```{r load-lib, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
# Add any other libraries here
library(dplyr)


```


```{r load-data, include=FALSE}
# load your data here and any pre-processing/cleaning 
#  that you need for your report.
df <- read_csv("data/hd_mortalitybyca.csv")
library(tidyverse)

# 1. Load data加载数据
df <- read_csv("data/hd_mortalitybyca.csv")
dz_codes <- read_csv("data/dz_codes.csv")

# 2. Create Council Area lookup table 制作地区和地区代码的对照表
area <- dz_codes %>%
  select(CA, CAName) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  drop_na(CA, CAName)

# 3. Clean and prepare mortality data 清洗死亡数据表
final_df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    year_provisional = str_ends(Year, "p"),
    year = as.integer(str_remove(Year, "p"))
  ) %>%
  rename(
    age_group = AgeGroup,
    gender = Sex,
    diagnosis = Diagnosis,
    deaths = NumberOfDeaths,
    crude_rate = CrudeRate,
    easr = EASR,
    ca = Ca
  ) %>%
  left_join(area, by = c("ca" = "CA")) %>%
  mutate(
    area = if_else(
      ca == "S92000003",
      "Scotland",
      CAName
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    year, year_provisional,
    ca, area,
    age_group, gender, diagnosis,
    deaths, crude_rate, easr
  )

# 4. Validate cleaned data 只是验证数据是否有异常
stopifnot(nrow(final_df) == nrow(df))
stopifnot(!anyNA(final_df$area))
stopifnot(!anyNA(final_df$year))

glimpse(final_df)
```


## Research Question

As the years change, how do demographic factors (age and gender) and geographical location (areas) influence the overall mortality rates of heart disease in Scotland? The reason is that it is important to understand these differences in public health. By identifying which demographic groups are most vulnerable and which regions experience higher mortality rates, policymakers and healthcare providers can better allocate resources and design targeted interventions to reduce heart disease mortality across Scotland.
```{r load-data-1, echo=FALSE}
#1.筛选出冠心病 filter CHD
chd_df <- final_df %>%
  filter(diagnosis == "Coronary Heart Disease")
```
```{r national-trend-plot, echo=FALSE}
#全国的趋势图
time_df <- chd_df %>%
  filter(
    area == "Scotland",
    age_group == "All Ages",
    gender == "All"
  ) %>%
  arrange(year)
#下面实现制图 这个图标是从2015 - 2024苏格兰全国因为冠心病死亡的人数
ggplot(time_df, aes(x = year, y = easr)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2024) +
  labs(
    title = "Coronary Heart Disease Mortality in Scotland",
    subtitle = "National mortality trend, 2015–2024",
    x = "Year",
    y = "European Age-Standardised Mortality Rate (per 100,000)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r geography-plot, echo=FALSE}
#下面制作地区的数据表
geographical_df <- chd_df %>%
  filter(
    year >= 2015,
    year <= 2023,
    area != "Scotland",
    age_group == "All Ages",
    gender == "All"
  ) %>%
  group_by(area) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_easr = mean(easr, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_easr))
geographical_highlight_df <- geographical_df %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_easr)) %>%
  mutate(
    rank = row_number(),
    highlight_group = case_when(
      rank <= 5 ~ "Top 5",
      rank > n() - 5 ~ "Bottom 5",
      TRUE ~ "Middle"
    )
  )
geographical_top_bottom <- geographical_highlight_df %>%
  filter(highlight_group != "Middle")
#下面进行地区-冠心病死亡的2015-2023年平均图表制作
ggplot(
  geographical_top_bottom,
  aes(
    x = reorder(area, mean_easr),
    y = mean_easr,
    fill = highlight_group
  )
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(mean_easr, 1)),
    hjust = -0.2,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Top 5" = "#D55E00",
      "Bottom 5" = "#0072B2"
    )
  ) +
  expand_limits(
    y = max(geographical_top_bottom$mean_easr) * 1.12
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Geographical Differences in CHD Mortality",
    subtitle = "Top 5 and Bottom 5 Council Areas, 2015–2023",
    x = "Council Area",
    y = "Mean annual EASR (per 100,000)",
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Unweighted arithmetic mean of annual EASRs."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )
```

### Linear Regression Analysis

Use the European age-standardised mortality rate (EASR) as our response variable.

```{r regression-data, echo=FALSE}
# Use the 10 selected Council Areas
regression_df <- chd_df %>%
  filter(
    year >= 2015,
    year <= 2023,
    area %in% geographical_top_bottom$area,
    age_group == "All Ages",
    gender == "All"
  )
```

### a simple linear regression model using only year to predict CHD mortality rates.

```{r simple-regression, echo=FALSE}
# Simple linear regression
model1 <- lm(easr ~ year, data = regression_df)

# Model results
summary(model1)
```

The following plot shows the observed mortality rates and the fitted regression line.

```{r simple-regression-plot, echo=FALSE}
ggplot(regression_df, aes(x = year, y = easr)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              color = "red") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2023) +
  labs(
    title = "Simple Linear Regression",
    subtitle = "CHD mortality rates in 10 Council Areas",
    x = "Year",
    y = "EASR (per 100,000)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Limitations of the Simple Model

 The simple linear regression plot shows a slight downward trend in CHD mortality rates between 2015 and 2023. However, the observed mortality rates vary considerably across Council Areas within the same year.

  This suggests that year alone may not adequately explain the variation in mortality rates.
Therefore, I choose to extend the model by including Council Area as an additional predictor.

### Multiple Linear Regression

The multiple linear regression model includes both year and Council Area.

This display the relationship between year and mortality rates while also accounting for differences between areas.

```{r multiple-regression, echo=FALSE}
# Multiple linear regression
model2 <- lm(easr ~ year + area, data = regression_df)

# Model results
summary(model2)
```

###  Multiple Regression Plot

use the fitted model to show the predicted mortality trends for each Council Area.

```{r multiple-regression-plot, echo=FALSE}
# Calculate predicted mortality rates
regression_df$predicted_easr <- predict(model2)

# Plot predicted trends for each area
ggplot(regression_df,
       aes(x = year, y = predicted_easr,
           color = area)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2023) +
  labs(
    title = "Multiple Linear Regression",
    subtitle = "Predicted CHD mortality trends by Council Area",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Predicted EASR (per 100,000)",
    color = "Council Area"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The fitted lines show the predicted mortality rates for the ten Council Areas.

Because the model uses a common year coefficient, the fitted lines have the same slope but different intercepts.

###  Actual vs Predicted Mortality Rates

```{r predicted-vs-actual, echo=FALSE}
ggplot(regression_df,
       aes(x = easr, y = predicted_easr)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
              linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs Predicted Mortality Rates",
    subtitle = "Multiple Linear Regression",
    x = "Actual EASR (per 100,000)",
    y = "Predicted EASR (per 100,000)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The dashed red line represents perfect predictions. Points closer to this line indicate smaller prediction errors.

###  Model Comparison

We compare the two models using and adjusted R-squared and residual standard error.

```{r regression-comparison, echo=FALSE}
# Compare model performance
comparison <- tibble(
  Model = c("Simple", "Multiple"),
  R_squared = c(
    summary(model1)$r.squared,
    summary(model2)$r.squared
  ),
  Adjusted_R_squared = c(
    summary(model1)$adj.r.squared,
    summary(model2)$adj.r.squared
  ),
  Residual_SE = c(
    sigma(model1),
    sigma(model2)
  )
)

# Display comparison table
knitr::kable(
  comparison,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Comparison of Linear Regression Models"
)
```
```{r gender+year model echo = off}
#整理数据 年龄分组
demographic_df <- chd_df %>%
  filter(
    area == "Scotland",
    year >= 2015,
    year <= 2023,
    age_group %in% c(
      "0-44 years",
      "45-64 years",
      "65-74 years",
      "75plus years"
    ),
    gender %in% c("Male", "Female")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    age_group = factor(
      age_group,
      levels = c(
        "0-44 years",
        "45-64 years",
        "65-74 years",
        "75plus years"
      )
    ),
#整理数据 性别分组
    gender = factor(
      gender,
      levels = c("Female", "Male")
    ),
    year_centered = year - 2015
  )

model3 <- lm(
  crude_rate ~ year_centered + age_group + gender,
  data = demographic_df
)

summary(model3)
#对建模的假设“不同年龄段男女死亡率差距固定”的检查
demographic_df %>%
  group_by(age_group, gender) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_rate = mean(crude_rate),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = gender,
    values_from = mean_rate
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    gap = Male - Female
  )
#通过检查结果可以知道实际上差距很大 因此我们要引入age和gender的交互项进行建模
```

```{r model4 echo = off}
#model4 
model4 <- lm(
  crude_rate ~ year_centered + age_group * gender,
  data = demographic_df
)

summary(model4)
#model4展现了良好的拟合效果Adjusted R-squared增加到了99%+ 但是仍然有问题 也即是假定0-44的女性死亡率每年下降 最终会导致负死亡率
```

```{r compare echo = off}
#比较模型model3 和model4
anova(model3, model4)
#通过比对数据可以发现 F = 136.84，p 极小，RSS（残差平方和显著减小）支持引入交互项
```


```{r Test}
diagnostic_df <- regression_df %>%
  mutate(
    fitted_value = fitted(model2),
    residual = residuals(model2)
  )
ggplot(
  diagnostic_df,
  aes(x = year, y = residual)
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "grey50"
  ) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~area, ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals over Time by Council Area",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Residual"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
autocorrelation_df <- diagnostic_df %>%
  group_by(area) %>%
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  summarise(
    lag1_cor = cor(
      residual,
      lag(residual),
      use = "complete.obs"
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(lag1_cor))

autocorrelation_df
x <- c(12, 8, 5, -3, -7)

lag(x)
```

A higher adjusted R-squared suggests that the model explains more variation after accounting for the number of predictors.

A lower residual standard error indicates that the fitted values are generally closer to the observed mortality rates.

These measures are able to assess whether adding Council Area improves the model.

### Discussion and Limitations

### Regression Results and Discussion

The simple linear regression model showed a weak relationship between year and CHD mortality rates, with an R-squared value of 0.017. This means that year alone explained only 1.7% of the variation in mortality rates across the selected Council Areas.

After adding Council Area to the multiple linear regression model, the R-squared increased to 0.743, and the adjusted R-squared increased from 0.006 to 0.711. The residual standard error also decreased from 32.986 to 17.796.

These results suggest that including geographical location substantially improved the model's fit. The multiple regression plot also shows clear differences in predicted mortality rates between Council Areas, while the overall trend decreases over time.

However, the analysis only includes ten Council Areas selected based on their mortality rates. Therefore, the findings may not represent all areas in Scotland.

## Data

The dataset for this investigation is the Scottish Heart Disease Statistics. I utilized the mortality data categorized by Council Areas and filtered for overall heart disease mortality. During the data wrangling process using the tidyverse package, I joined the raw mortality data with the Data Zone Codes dictionary to convert alphanumeric zone codes into readable Council Area names. I also removed missing values 'NA' to maintain data quality.

The final cleaned dataset focuses on four key variables for our investigation:
1. Year: The variable tracking mortality trends.
2. Gender: A variable differentiating male and female mortality.
3. Age_group: Demographic brackets (0-44 years, 45-64 years, 65-74 years, under 75 years and 75+ years).
4. Area: The Scottish Council Areas, which is necessary for regional comparison.
